notes.text: A virtuous woman — Here he lays down several qualifications of an excellent wife, which are delivered in alphabetical order, each verse beginning with a several letter of the Hebrew alphabet.
No need — He shall have no need to use indirect courses to get wealth.

Flax — That she may find employment for her servants. Worketh - She encourages them to work by her example; which was a common practice among princesses in those first ages. Not that it is the duty of kings and queens to use manual operations, but it is the duty of all persons, the greatest not excepted, to improve all their talents, and particularly their time, which is one of the noblest of them, to the service of that God to whom they must give an account, and to the good of that community to which they are related.
From afar — By the sale of her home-spun commodities she purchases the choicest goods which come from far countries.
Giveth — Distributes all necessary provisions.
Considereth — Whether it be fit for her use. The fruit - With the effects of her diligence. Planteth - She improves the land to the best advantage.

Girdeth — She uses great diligence and expedition in her employment; for which end, men in those times used to gird up their long and loose garments about their loins. Strengtheneth - Puts forth her utmost strength in her business.
Perceiveth — She finds great comfort in her labours. Her candle - Which is not to be taken strictly, but only signifies her unwearied care and industry.

She layeth — By her own example she provokes her servants to labour. And although in these latter and more delicate times, such mean employments are grown out of fashion among great persons, yet they were not so in former ages, neither in other countries, nor in this land; whence all women unmarried unto this day are called in the language of our law, Spinsters.
Not afraid — Of any injuries of the weather. Are clothed - She hath provided enough, not only for their necessity, but also for their delight and ornament.
Tapestry — For the furniture of her house. Silk - Which was agreeable to her high quality.
It known — Observed and respected, not only for his own worth, but for his wife's sake. Sitteth - In counsel or judgment.
Girdles — Curiously wrought of linen, and gold, or other precious materials.

Strength — Strength of mind, magnanimity, courage, activity. Her clothing - Her ornament and glory. Rejoice - She lives in constant tranquillity of mind, from a just confidence in God's gracious providence.

Openeth her mouth — She is neither sullenly silent, nor full of impertinent talk, but speaks discreetly and piously, as occasion offers. In her tongue - Her speeches are guided by wisdom and grace, and not by inordinate passions. And this practice is called a law in her tongue, because it is constant and customary, and proceeds from an inward and powerful principle of true wisdom.
Looketh well — She diligently observes the management of her domestick business, and the whole carriage of her children and servants.

favour — Comeliness, which commonly gives women favour with those who behold them. Deceitful - It gives a false representation of the person, being often a cover to a deformed soul; it does not give a man that satisfaction, which at first he promised to himself from it; and it is soon lost, not only by death, but by many diseases and contingencies.

Give her — It is but just, that she should enjoy those praises which her labours deserve. Let her works - If men be silent, the lasting effects of her prudence and diligence will trumpet forth her praises. In the gates - In the most publick and solemn assemblies.

glossa.text:
*A strong woman.* Thus far the words of king Lamuel, etc., *as far as* the virtues and the rewards be described.

*Who shall find a strong woman.* The strong woman is the holy Church, etc., *as far as* he granted to preach throughout the world, he added:

*The heart of her husband trusteth in her.* The husband, the redeemer, etc., *as far as* when through the preachers he calls back to the truth those whom he had deceived.

*And he shall have no need of spoils.* Because the Church shall never cease to restore to the faith of Christ the souls deceived by the devil, until, the course of the world being finished, the number of the just be completed. But because whatsoever of good the holy Church or the faithful soul does, it receives from above, it is rightly subjoined:
*She will render him good and not evil.* The soul will render good to Christ, etc., *as far as* to which is like, *let us serve him,* etc.
*She hath sought.* By what works, etc., *as far as* concerning this recompense it is more openly subjoined:

*She is become as a merchant's ship from afar.* A sailor is called *institor,* because he presses on diligently to the acquiring of wares, etc., *as far as* of whom it is said: *Amen I say to you, they have received their reward.*

*By night.* As the whole course of the present world, etc., *as far as* and to practise such things in secret.

*She hath risen.* When some faithful man girds himself solicitously to take the care of his neighbours. Which he does in two ways, because he both calls to the faith those who wander without; and those who are in the faith, that they may press on more in works; whence he subjoins:

*And she hath given a prey to her household.* He gives a prey to his household, when he reconciles those whom the devil snatched away to the fellowship of them that went before in the faith. He gives food to his handmaids, when he refreshes with the remembrance of the reward all the humble, and those keeping the commands through fear, lest they grow weary in godly labour.

*She hath considered.* To-day and even to the end of the world the strong woman, etc., *as far as* what is the fulness of beatitude in the kingdom of God.

*Of the fruit of her hands.* Because from the fruit-bearing deeds of her own faithful ones, etc., *as far as* and she labours for them what she can.
*She hath girded.* When she prepares herself for the works of the virtues, etc., *as far as* that you may shine with good works.
*She hath tasted and seen that it is good.* Of that field, namely, etc., *as far as* so but also by night, the lamp being lighted, she works with her hands.

*She hath put out her hand.* He means strong things, works perfected in charity, etc., *as far as* of whose strength it is said: *The kingdom of heaven suffereth violence, and the violent bear it away ((Matth. XI))*.

*And her fingers,* he says, *have taken hold of the spindle.* The distaff in the left hand, the spindle in the right, etc., *as far as* but what the strong woman, namely the holy Church or the perfect soul, has wrought by the spindle; he subjoins:
*She hath opened her hand to the needy, and her palms.* This concerning alms, etc., *as far as* when far and wide she scattered preachers unto the nations that lack eternal salvation.

*She shall not fear.* The colds of snow, etc., *as far as* because she believed God saying that *the gates of hell shall not prevail against her ((Matth. XVI))*.

*For all her household are clothed with double garments,* etc. With wisdom, namely, for the unmasking of heresies, and with patience for the bearing of the battles of open enemies, etc., *as far as* who is deservedly bound in the cold, because he had not the garment of piety.
*An embroidered garment.* An embroidered garment is that which, with varying texture, is wont to be wrought most firm, etc., *as far as* for the fine linens are the justifications of the saints.
*Her husband is noble in the gates.* The husband is the Lord who was seen to be ignoble, etc., *as far as* he shall appear sublime unto all.
*She made fine linen and sold it.* In the cloth of fine linen, etc., *as far as* for the nations passed over from vices to virtues, from the devil to Christ.
*Strength.* Strength for enduring, etc., *as far as* be thou strong against backbiters.

*Her mouth.* For this only, in speaking, she opened her mouth, etc., *as far as* to each belongs that which he subjoins:

*The law of clemency.* That she may not punish at once, as the law of Moses, etc., *as far as* and so he absolved her: *Go, and sin no more.*

*She hath considered.* Because she subtly searches out all the thoughts of her own conscience, etc., *as far as* and ceases not to practise the things which she has learned are to be done.

*She hath not eaten her bread idle.* Because she fulfils in work the sacred word which she receives, etc., *as far as* not only idle, but wordy and curious.
*Her children rose up.* Which he knew as a prophet was to come, etc., *as far as* but in the judgment he will show how great is the glory of his own resurrection.

*Many daughters have gathered together riches: thou hast surpassed them all.* The Churches of the heretics, etc., *as far as* which with chaste faith and perfect work follows the footsteps of her Redeemer.
*Favour is deceitful and beauty is vain.* The glory of praise is deceitful, etc., *as far as* for he shows in what manner he praises her, *Give her of the fruit.*
*Give her of the fruit of her hands.* This that husband, of whom it was said above, etc., *as far as* and with God approving and rewarding, to whom is honour and glory.

notes.text: Blessed — The Hebrew words are very emphatical: O the blessedness of that man! Counsel - That doth not lead his life according to their counsel, or manner of living. Standeth - Which notes a more settled abode in it. Way - In their manner of conversation. Seat - Which notes a constant and resolved perseverance in their wicked courses. Scornful - Of those who make a mock of sin, and scoff at goodness and goodmen. Divers observe a gradation in this verse; the following clause still exceeding the former, for standing is more than walking, and sitting more than standing; and sinners in scripture use, are worse than the ungodly, and the scornful are the worst of sinners.
Day and night — Not seldom and slightly, but diligently, and constantly.
Whither — His happiness is not short and transitory, but, like those trees which are continually green and flourishing.
Ungodly — Their condition is far different. Chaff - They are restless and unquiet: their seeming felicity, hath no firm foundation, but quickly vanishes and flees away as chaff before the wind.
Not stand — Not endure the trial. Judgment - In the great and general judgment of the world.

Knoweth — He approves, loves, and delights in them, and therefore will recompence them. Perish - All their designs and courses shall come to nothing, and they shall perish with them. There is nothing in this psalm which is not applicable to Christ, but some things which are not all applicable to David. Threatenings denounced against the adversaries of Christ's kingdom, ver. 1-6. Promises made to Christ, ver. 7-9. Counsel given to all, to submit to him, ver. 10-12.

glossa.text: « Blessed is the man who hath not gone away, etc. » ((AUG., Enarr. in Psal., tom. III.)) The order, Adam went away when he withdrew from God; he stood, when he was delighted with sin; he sat, when, confirmed in pride, he could not return, save as set free by this man, who had none of these things. Adam went away when he consented to the persuasion of the devil; he stood, while he ate the apple; he sat, while he excused himself: « The woman whom thou gavest me seduced me. » ((Gen. III)) . After the likeness of exiles, who, while they are on the road, are more easily called back, while they now stand, with more difficulty: at length with the greatest difficulty, when they have there been made masters and lords. ((REMI.)) There is sinning by thought, by act, and by words in teaching. ((CASS.)) The impious man is so against God, the sinner against himself, the pestilent man against his neighbour. « In the chair, giving an example of sinning. » ((CASS.)) The throne is of kings, the tribunal of judges, the chair properly of teachers. ((Ibid.)) It is as though he said: You who have fallen through the first Adam, be ye conformed to this second one: because the blessed man is the contrary of the first

« But in the law. » AUG. ((CASS.)) Here he is shown full of every good in himself. ((AUG.)) It is not perfect praise to flee the things to be blamed, unless the things to be praised follow. In the order in which they grew in the first man, they are taken away in the second.

« In the law. » ((Ibid.)) He who is in the law acts according to the law, he who is under the law is acted upon according to the law: the one is free, the other a slave. ((Ibid. AMBR.)) One thing is the law which is written for him that serves, another that which is beheld with the mind by him who has no need of letters. « The will. » ((CASS.)) That there be no weariness of labour, nor idleness, but he shall meditate always. The will of sense is under the law; of reason, in the law; of divinity, above the law.

« And he shall be. » ((Ibid.)) Here he is shown useful to us, giving the fruit of life, and leaves, and overshadowing us, « Blessed is the man. But in the law. And he shall be. » The full definition of the blessed man. All these things belong not to every blessed man, but to Christ alone. « As a tree. » ((Ibid.)) After the likeness of the tree of life which is in paradise, whereof obedient man was to have eaten. « A tree. » ((Ibid.)) In paradise there is the tree of life, a tree unto life, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. « Of waters. » ((AUG.)) The waters are the Holy Spirit, according to that word: « He that shall have believed in me, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water ((Joan. VII)), » and it is against the heats of the vices. ((CASS.)) Or, by water, the wisdom of God, by which the inner man is restored, as thirst by water. ((AUG.)) Or the mortal race, as Job: « Many waters, many peoples, » because they flow down into death, as waters into the sea. « He shall give. » ((Ibid.)) To give pertains to the rational sense and to the will of the one offering. « And the leaf. » ((Ibid.)) As the leaves cover the fruit, so the words of the Lord guard his promises. « And all things. » ((Ibid.)) Why go through them one by one.

« Not so the impious. » Here by the vengeance upon the wicked he terrifies the adverse, the dread of these makes what has gone before more welcome. « From the face of the earth. » ((AUG.)) Of eternal stability, because as this earth nourishes and holds up a man, so that other earth holds up the inner man.

« Therefore they shall not rise again. » Because the wind casteth them away, that is, therefore, because they have been given over to a reprobate sense: therefore they do not rise again in the first resurrection, that they may judge themselves in counsel, that they may set the wills of God before their own. Or in the council, that is, in the harmonious multitude of the just, the impious idolaters, or apostates. Sinners, false Christians: or else therefore they do not rise again in the time to come, that they may judge, or that, being judged, they may rest in the council, that is, in the college of the just. « In judgment, etc. » In the judgment there will be four orders: some shall judge and shall not be judged, as the most perfect; some shall neither judge nor be judged, as the damned unbelievers; some shall be judged and shall be saved, as the moderately good; some shall be judged and shall perish, as the evil faithful. « In the council. » ((AUG.)) In the eternal good, to follow which was counsel to the saints. « Or in the council, » in the judgment, that they may judge together with them; for there is judgment when different sins are punished with different penalties; and it is said from this by likeness. « They rise again. » What resurrections these are: of the soul, from sins in the present; of the body, from death in the time to come, whereby it shall be made impassible and immortal.
« For the Lord knoweth, etc., » That is, these do not rise again in the soul, because God does not approve their works, but those of the just only.

notes.text: Let him show his wisdom as well as his faith by his works; not by words only.

If ye have bitter zeal — True Christian zeal is only the flame of love. Even in your hearts - Though it went no further. Do not lie against the truth - As if such zeal could consist with heavenly wisdom.

This wisdom — Which is consistent with such zeal. Is earthly - Not heavenly; not from the Father of Lights. Animal - Not spiritual; not from the Spirit of God. Devilish - Not the gift of Christ, but such as Satan breathes into the soul.

But the wisdom from above is first pure — From all that is earthly, natural, devilish. Then peaceable - True peace attending purity, it is quiet, inoffensive. Gentle - Soft, mild, yielding, not rigid. Easy to be entreated - To be persuaded, or convinced; not stubborn, sour, or morose. Full of good fruits - Both in the heart and in the life, two of which are immediately specified. Without partiality - Loving all, without respect of persons; embracing all good things, rejecting all evil. And without dissimulation - Frank, open.

And the principle productive of this righteousness is sown, like good seed, in the peace of a believer's mind, and brings forth a plentiful harvest of happiness, (which is the proper fruit of righteousness,) for them that make peace — That labour to promote this pure and holy peace among all men.

From whence come wars and fightings — Quarrels and wars among you, quite opposite to this peace? Is it not from your pleasures - Your desires of earthly pleasures. Which war - Against your souls. In your members - Here is the first seat of the war. Hence proceeds the war of man with man, king with king, nation with nation.

Ye kill — In your heart, for "he that hateth his brother is a murderer." Ye fight and war - That is, furiously strive and contend. Ye ask not - And no marvel; for a man full of evil desire, of envy or hatred, cannot pray.
But if ye do ask, ye receive not, because ye ask amiss — That is, from a wrong motive.

glossa.text: *Who is a wise man and endued with knowledge among you?* Those being confuted who have neither holiness of life nor continence of tongue, he admonishes those who seemed to themselves wise, or even were so, that they should show wisdom rather by living in discipline than by teaching others, because he who is more inclined to teaching than to doing sometimes incurs boasting, or contention, or envy against other teachers, and many other evils.
*And be liars against the truth.* Do not lie to God, to whom in baptism you promised to renounce the pomps of the devil, which you do not do when you wish to be proud of good things.

*But that which.* This is the meekness which he commanded above was to be had, contrary to bitterness of zeal and to contentions. *First indeed it is chaste.* Unless chastity first sit in the mind, no perfection will follow in the work. *Easy to be persuaded, consenting to good things.* If he does aught the less, whether through ignorance or through negligence, he yields assent to the persuasion of good men.

*But the fruit.* After he had distinguished wisdom through the several virtues; that he may the more easily invite to it, he subjoins its fruit: *It is sown in peace.* He does not demand to seem more learned or more holy than he is: he does not tear his neighbour for his own commendation, which contentious wisdom does. Not only for the aforesaid things ought a man to seek wisdom of this sort, but also for this; because by those who make peace, as by those who cast it, this seed is sown, and there is prepared in peace the fruit of eternal blessedness, that is the reward of justice, which is repaid for just works. He therefore who here is zealous for peace, and sprinkles the ground of his heart with the works of peace as with seed, it is just that he should have eternal peace, as the fruit of this seed.

*From whence wars,* etc. ((BED.)) He had forbidden zeal and contention, whence he disputes yet more at large, adding other vices which follow from it: from contention, concupiscence, from concupiscences, wars and strifes. For he who desires to be preferred, or to abound in temporal things, hates, envies, kills.

*Because that.* On account of these things, namely that you ask God worthily *postulatis*; read *non postulatis*, "you ask not"; for if you were to ask him with devout intercession, he would give also the temporal things necessary for use, and not the everlasting only.

notes.text: They passed through Galilee — Though not through the cities, but by them, in the most private ways. He was not willing that any should know it: for he taught his disciples - He wanted to be alone with them some time, in order to instruct them fully concerning his sufferings. The Son of man is delivered - It is as sure as if it were done already. Matt. xvii, 22; Luke ix, 44.

They understood not the word — They did not understand how to reconcile the death of our saviour (nor consequently his resurrection, which supposed his death) with their notions of his temporal kingdom.
Luke ix, 46.
Who should be greatest — Prime minister in his kingdom.
Let him be the least of all — Let him abase himself the most.
Matt. xviii, 2; Luke ix, 47.
One such little child — Either in years or in heart.

glossa.text: *They shall kill him,* etc. He mingles sad things with prosperous, that when they come they may not be borne with unprepared minds. If it saddens them that he is to be killed, it ought to gladden them that on the third day he is to rise again.

*They knew not.* Not so much from slowness of wit as from love: because they had known him to be true God, they could not believe that he would die. And because they were accustomed to speak to them in figures, shuddering at his death, they thought that in these things also he spoke figuratively.

*Capharnaum. ((HIER.))* The village of consolation: it agrees with the foregoing sentence: *Being slain, on the third day he shall rise again ((Joan. XII))*. The grain of wheat dies, that it may be gathered more manifoldly: if it does not die, it remains alone. *What in the way,* etc. In the way they were treating of the primacy: a treating suited to the place. For a princedom is entered by force, and so is forsaken, and while it is held it slips away: and it is uncertain in what lodging, that is, on what day, it shall be ended; whence he says: *He that will be first,* etc.

*They had disputed among themselves. ((BEDA.))* Hence the dispute seems to have arisen, because they had seen Peter and James and John led apart into the mountain, and that some secret had there been entrusted to them; and to Peter also, as Matthew says, the keys of the kingdom of heaven promised, and the Church to be built upon the rock of faith, from which he himself received his name. They thought therefore either that those three were set before the rest, or that Peter was set before them all.

*And sitting down,* etc. They as they went were disputing about the primacy, and he, sitting, teaches humility. For princes toil, the humble are at rest. He wills to heal the desire of glory by humility, and first admonishes by a simple command, then by the example of a child's innocence.
*Having embraced him.* He signifies that the humble are worthy of his embrace, who can rightly glory and say: *His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me ((Cant. II))*.

*Whosoever shall receive one.* Either he shows simply that the poor of Christ are to be received by those who would be greater, for his honour. Or he persuades them to be themselves little ones in malice, that they may be simple as little ones. *And whosoever.* Because he was teaching that he is received in the children, as the head in the members, lest this only should be thought to be what appeared, he added: *And whosoever shall receive me,* etc.

*He answered him.* Because he had said: *Whosoever shall receive one of such children, receiveth me,* John understands that they who do not walk sincerely do not receive them in his name; whence he says: *Master, we saw a certain man.* As if he said: This man ought not to be received in thy name. *And we forbade him.* He thought that one who does not use the office was to be shut out from the benefit; but he is taught that no one is to be barred from the good which he has in part, but rather to be urged on to that which he has not: whence: *Forbid him not.*

glossa.text: *And covenants.* We have struck a league with death, and with hell we have made a pact.
*For they have said.* ((RAB.)) The voice of the lost, etc., *as far as* and we shall be brought to nothing.

notes.text: Name — By thy own strength. Judge - Plead my cause.
Strangers — The Zephites, whom, though Israelites, he calls strangers in regard of their barbarous and perfidious carriage.

Thy truth — Whereby thou art engaged to fulfil thy promises and threatenings. David complains to God, ver. 1-8. Prays for help against his enemies, ver. 9-15. Assures himself of God's protection, ver. 16- 18. And their destruction, ver. 19-23. To the chief musician on Neginoth, Maschil, A psalm of David.

glossa.text: *The Ziphites.* ((HIER., AUG.)) They are interpreted the flourishing ones *Florente*, etc., *as far as* he admonishes us to praise God in adversities.

*O God, in thy name.* ((AUG.)) He prays among the Ziphites. ((AUG., HIER.)) Here, save me in thy name; afterwards, I fear not to be judged in thy strength. ((AUG.)) O God, in thy name: the words of the Church hiding among the Ziphites, whose good is within and whose reward is hidden; others ask to be delivered by other means: I, in thy name.

*O God, hear.* ((CASS.)) Again God, a name of power; he repeats it that the help may not be slow. *Give ear,* ((AUG.)) The Ziphites, even if they hear these things, yet do not understand, who know nothing except things temporal.
*Strangers.* ((AUG.)) Ziph was a hamlet which belonged to the tribe of Juda, whence the Ziphites.

*For behold.* ((CASS.)) Diapsalmus. What God does for him and for the Ziphites, whence he pays his praises. *He helpeth.* ((AUG.)) Which they themselves know not, among whom I lie hid; but this, that he helps me, they would see, if they set God before their eyes.

*Turn back the evils upon mine enemies. ((Ibid.))* Or, turn back: he prays for such as are to be converted; and this is the victim which he pays for his deliverance. *In thy truth.* ((AUG.)) Or according to another reading: *In thy strength,* destroy those whom in thy weakness thou hast borne with. *I will freely sacrifice. ((Ibid.))* Because for his own sake, not for anything else that I might wish from him. He who praises for the sake of something else praises of necessity; if he had that thing, he would not praise. *But to me,* and the things he gave are pleasing for the giver's sake.

notes.text: They passed through Galilee — Though not through the cities, but by them, in the most private ways. He was not willing that any should know it: for he taught his disciples - He wanted to be alone with them some time, in order to instruct them fully concerning his sufferings. The Son of man is delivered - It is as sure as if it were done already. Matt. xvii, 22; Luke ix, 44.

They understood not the word — They did not understand how to reconcile the death of our saviour (nor consequently his resurrection, which supposed his death) with their notions of his temporal kingdom.
Luke ix, 46.
Who should be greatest — Prime minister in his kingdom.
Let him be the least of all — Let him abase himself the most.
Matt. xviii, 2; Luke ix, 47.
One such little child — Either in years or in heart.

glossa.text: *They shall kill him,* etc. He mingles sad things with prosperous, that when they come they may not be borne with unprepared minds. If it saddens them that he is to be killed, it ought to gladden them that on the third day he is to rise again.

*They knew not.* Not so much from slowness of wit as from love: because they had known him to be true God, they could not believe that he would die. And because they were accustomed to speak to them in figures, shuddering at his death, they thought that in these things also he spoke figuratively.

*Capharnaum. ((HIER.))* The village of consolation: it agrees with the foregoing sentence: *Being slain, on the third day he shall rise again ((Joan. XII))*. The grain of wheat dies, that it may be gathered more manifoldly: if it does not die, it remains alone. *What in the way,* etc. In the way they were treating of the primacy: a treating suited to the place. For a princedom is entered by force, and so is forsaken, and while it is held it slips away: and it is uncertain in what lodging, that is, on what day, it shall be ended; whence he says: *He that will be first,* etc.

*They had disputed among themselves. ((BEDA.))* Hence the dispute seems to have arisen, because they had seen Peter and James and John led apart into the mountain, and that some secret had there been entrusted to them; and to Peter also, as Matthew says, the keys of the kingdom of heaven promised, and the Church to be built upon the rock of faith, from which he himself received his name. They thought therefore either that those three were set before the rest, or that Peter was set before them all.

*And sitting down,* etc. They as they went were disputing about the primacy, and he, sitting, teaches humility. For princes toil, the humble are at rest. He wills to heal the desire of glory by humility, and first admonishes by a simple command, then by the example of a child's innocence.
*Having embraced him.* He signifies that the humble are worthy of his embrace, who can rightly glory and say: *His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me ((Cant. II))*.

*Whosoever shall receive one.* Either he shows simply that the poor of Christ are to be received by those who would be greater, for his honour. Or he persuades them to be themselves little ones in malice, that they may be simple as little ones. *And whosoever.* Because he was teaching that he is received in the children, as the head in the members, lest this only should be thought to be what appeared, he added: *And whosoever shall receive me,* etc.

*He answered him.* Because he had said: *Whosoever shall receive one of such children, receiveth me,* John understands that they who do not walk sincerely do not receive them in his name; whence he says: *Master, we saw a certain man.* As if he said: This man ought not to be received in thy name. *And we forbade him.* He thought that one who does not use the office was to be shut out from the benefit; but he is taught that no one is to be barred from the good which he has in part, but rather to be urged on to that which he has not: whence: *Forbid him not.*

registers.label: Spare
lines: They argued on the road about who was the greatest.
Jesus set a child among them.
Whoever would be first must be last of all.
And servant of all.
Welcome one small child in my name,
and you welcome the One who sent me.
Come, let us worship in the lowest place.
We come to serve. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: They were arguing about who was greatest, and Jesus took a little child and stood her in the middle of them and gathered her into his arms.
Whoever welcomes the child welcomes God.
This is the wisdom from above — not the kind that pushes to the front, but the kind that is gentle, peaceable, willing to be last.
Whoever welcomes the child welcomes God.
So come down from the high places. Take the lowest seat. Reach for the ones the world overlooks.
Whoever welcomes the child welcomes God.
For God is our helper, and the harvest of righteousness is sown in peace. Come, let us worship.
Whoever welcomes the child welcomes God. Amen.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: The disciples wanted to be greatest.
We come to serve.
Jesus set a child in their midst.
We come to serve.
The first must be last, the servant of all.
We come to serve.
Come, let us worship from the lowest place.
We welcome the child, and welcome God. Amen.
